content: Scrivener's widow and landlady in Great St Helen's
Makes oak-gall ink and keeps the bread-board notch
A dropped pan is already a demand, and money not yet had is not a dinner.
She prices a short loaf at a finger and a play that begins in a broken oath at a pin, and she asks the question while her hands are full.
At the Mayor's porch she says the City in one sentence.
When she names a man who stands near power, she lowers her voice and will not admit she has done it.
She will keep a slice back and stand over him until he has eaten it.
She knows what Anne meant by the kind with two ends, and she will not be the one to say it.
She will bring a sermon home complete, and she will not let a player past the chair while you are in the bed.
She will name sixpence and not take it off the plate, and she will not send an unfolded leaf to the Bell.
She will not buy a second loaf to mend a finger, and she will not send a letter a day before the carrier is in.
She will not have the manner of a bad day's news in her kitchen.
She will accuse nobody when a spoon is short, and she can bear being the one who misplaced it.
She pays for the work she orders, and she rates three discarded leaves by what they held up.
She will take two houses alike as no plot, and she will not ask a second time for a letter you have left shut.
She will call a clear board repentance, sell you the quire she has by her, and not ask the coffer's figure.
She boiled Monday's ink from your own receipt, counted threepence when you sat on Thursday, and would not have a sermon made of the short loaf.
She took two threepences, would not make a sermon of a short loaf, and was not told what Saturday's part came to.

She counts a quarter twice, writes the receipt in her husband's law-hand, and will not let the empty chamber to a man who burns more candle than you do. The blessing she gives with the beer is not a plot.
A twelvemonth, called short, stopped her for a herring. She took the threepence and did not ask for a new count.
She will not hear Anne's sentence improved, and she keeps the penny loaf at a finger and a half until she chooses to leave it alone.
On Easter she leaves the penny loaf unmeasured, and on the next day she is back to a finger and a half.
She allows one bough and no ribbon, and she does not want a wood.

One bough, and no woodland. Three pence when you sit, and the three pence stays in the pot when you do not. She will take a death in the second act as sense. She will not give a verdict without a plot.
Threepence when you sit. She will take a death in the second act. She will not have a sermon in a letter. She hopes the ground is not the point, and she does not say whose the crown is.
She boils the Monday ink, prices the loaf at a penny and a finger and a half, and does not weigh it.
She measures the loaf at a finger and a half and will not obey a paper she has not got.
She will hide a lodger and swear the house before she will discuss him. The latch stays as it always was.
She shut the house, lodger included, to anything west of the Stocks for the rest of the month, and on Saturday she still did not have the plot of the king.
She heard the king with the knife down, called the uneasy reign a bad example, and would not show it this month.
At the window she said that is not how you ask for bread, and she barred the shutter, not the street door.
She will bar a door and talk about the heat, so that a frightened house still sounds like her house.
She can hear a plot once and know which man in it has sense, and she can measure a loaf without changing its price.
She will name a thatch and still give no ruling on the next day, which she had not done before.
She takes offence when a pack is called heavy, and she will allow a plot if the man arrives.
She welcomes a lodger by handing him the washing, and she stops a plot at the sum.
Fairings rot the teeth, by her rule, and a man holding the stair-post is sent up.
She distrusts an afternoon with no walking in it, and a short letter, by her rule, has less room for lies.
A friar who marries without the fathers' leave is, by her rule, no better than the Nurse, and the end she names is a churchyard.
In her parish a noise is a charge, and she will shift her feet when the glass turns.
A tooth black at the neck settles, by her word, when it is in a dish.
A penny is the whole of the business on her board, and the loaf is a full thumb short.
A penny is still the loaf, a full thumb short, and she will not measure it twice for a Sunday face.
Board is threepence when he sits to it, and she will not make a week out of one dinner.
She has finished with remedies. The jaw is a quince, the cure is a shilling and a walk of forty yards, and she will mention both at every meal until Thursday has passed.
She counts candles as candles. Three on Tuesday were the tooth. One at dawn was the lovers. She will not let the two numbers become one, and she will not let a share become a coffer.
She will boil a supper down to nothing and then tell you the food has done more yielding than you have.
She will spare a length of thread and not the basket, and she will not have a play brought to her board.
She took the short loaf's answer as sound doctrine and said she would not ask twice.
She will fill the horn on a Monday and she will not take a plot with the copperas.
She will let you carry the stores, and she will not let you write the price.
She will approve a play in which tradesmen play at playing, and she has already called the fairies popery.
The sixpence is the firing. She will not give a third candle. The loaf stays two fingers short, and a penny.
She had never been inside a playhouse, and she went once, in her church hat, and at the door she had nothing to say but good night.
Mistress Ansell has been inside a playhouse once. She will not go again. Once is knowledge for her, and twice would be appetite. She does not require a report of a parlour.
She will not bake on a rumour, and she will not spend her playhouse sentence a second time in a porch.
She will not take money for the house's latch, and the receipt for the quarter is in her husband's law-hand.
She will call a morning comedy from the sound of the feet, and she will not judge a play that has no ending.
